lesson.title: CRISPR-Cas9: Precision Editing Borrowed from Bacteria
lesson.summary: CRISPR-Cas9 is a genome editing tool, adapted from a natural bacterial immune system, that uses a short guide RNA to direct the Cas9 enzyme to cut DNA at a specific, chosen location.
lesson.body:
Bacteria are under constant attack from viruses called bacteriophages, and over evolutionary time many bacteria and archaea evolved a remarkable adaptive immune system to fight back. When a bacterium survives an infection, it can capture a short piece of the invading virus's DNA and store it in its own genome, in a region made of repeated sequences called CRISPR, which stands for clustered regularly interspaced short palindromic repeats. If the same virus attacks again, the bacterium copies these stored snippets into short RNA molecules and uses a CRISPR associated protein, such as Cas9, to scan the cell for matching viral DNA and destroy it. In effect, bacteria keep a molecular mugshot file of their past attackers.

Around 2012, researchers including Jennifer Doudna and Emmanuelle Charpentier showed that this natural defense system could be simplified and repurposed as a programmable gene editing tool, work recognized with the 2020 Nobel Prize in Chemistry. The key insight is that the RNA piece guiding Cas9 does not have to come from a real virus. Scientists can design a short guide RNA with any sequence they choose, and because RNA bases pair with complementary DNA bases according to the same base pairing rules that govern DNA replication, that guide RNA will lead Cas9 to whatever DNA sequence in the genome matches it. This is what makes CRISPR so different from older gene editing tools built around recombinant DNA technology, such as restriction enzymes, which only cut at a small number of fixed recognition sequences. With CRISPR, changing the target is as simple as changing the guide RNA's sequence.

Once the guide RNA and Cas9 protein find their matching site in the genome, Cas9 acts as a pair of molecular scissors, cutting both strands of the DNA double helix and creating what is called a double strand break. What happens next depends entirely on the cell's own DNA repair machinery, the same machinery normally used to fix accidental damage. Most of the time, the break is patched by a fast but error prone pathway called non homologous end joining, or NHEJ, which simply stitches the cut ends back together and often leaves behind small insertions or deletions. If those extra or missing bases fall inside a gene's coding sequence, they can shift its reading frame and disable the gene entirely, which is useful when the goal is simply to knock a gene out. If instead a researcher supplies a matching piece of template DNA alongside the CRISPR machinery, the cell can sometimes use a more precise repair pathway called homology directed repair, or HDR, to copy the new sequence directly into the break site. HDR is how CRISPR can correct a specific mutation rather than just disrupting a gene, though it happens less efficiently than NHEJ and mainly in actively dividing cells.

CRISPR is not perfect. A guide RNA can occasionally bind to a DNA sequence that is similar but not identical to its intended target, producing an unwanted cut elsewhere in the genome, an issue researchers call an off target effect. Improving the specificity of guide RNAs and the fidelity of Cas9 variants remains an active area of research, and it is one of the reasons CRISPR based treatments are tested so carefully before they reach patients, a topic taken up directly in the next chapter on gene therapy.
